history.heading: Ancient Georgia
paragraphs: Georgia, at the crossroads of Europe and Asia in the Caucasus, has some of the oldest human fossils outside Africa, found at Dmanisi and about 1.8 million years old. It also has the oldest known evidence of winemaking, dating to around 6000 BCE.

In antiquity the kingdoms of Colchis, the land of the Golden Fleece in Greek myth, and Iberia (Kartli) existed. Kartli adopted Christianity in the early 4th century, making Georgia one of the first Christian nations, traditionally through Saint Nino.

history.heading: Golden Age and foreign domination
paragraphs: King David IV the Builder united Georgia in the early 12th century, and under Queen Tamar it enjoyed a golden age of power and culture, when Shota Rustaveli wrote the epic The Knight in the Panther's Skin.
Mongol invasions in the 13th century ended this era. Georgia was later divided and contested by the Ottoman and Persian empires. In 1801 the Russian Empire annexed eastern Georgia and later the rest.

history.heading: Soviet era and independence
paragraphs: Georgia declared independence in 1918, but the Red Army invaded in 1921, and it became part of the Soviet Union; Joseph Stalin was Georgian. In 1989 Soviet troops killed protesters in Tbilisi, and Georgia declared independence in 1991.

Wars in the early 1990s left the regions of Abkhazia and South Ossetia outside government control. The peaceful Rose Revolution of 2003 brought reformist Mikheil Saakashvili to power. In 2008 a short war with Russia ended with Russia recognising Abkhazia and South Ossetia as independent states, which most of the world considers occupied Georgian territory.

history.heading: Recent years
paragraphs: Georgian Dream, a party founded by billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, has governed since 2012. Georgia received EU candidate status in December 2023, but in 2024 the government passed a "foreign agents" law and suspended EU accession talks, triggering months of mass protests.

culture.heading: Language and faith
paragraphs: Georgian is a Kartvelian language with its own unique alphabet, one of only 14 in the world. The Georgian Orthodox Church is central to national identity; the country is dotted with ancient monasteries and churches, such as Jvari and Gelati.
Georgian polyphonic singing is recognised by UNESCO.

culture.heading: Wine and the supra
paragraphs: The traditional method of making wine in qvevri, clay vessels buried underground, is recognised by UNESCO. The supra, a feast led by a toastmaster (tamada) who gives elaborate toasts, is central to social life.
Georgian cuisine includes khachapuri (cheese bread), khinkali (dumplings), churchkhela (a sweet of nuts and grape juice) and dishes with walnuts and spices. Rugby, wrestling and chess are popular.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Georgia is a parliamentary republic. Since 2024 the president is elected indirectly by an electoral college. The prime minister leads the government. The disputed 2024 parliamentary elections, won by Georgian Dream, were rejected by the opposition and criticised by Western observers, and many opposition figures and protesters have been arrested.

The constitution commits Georgia to integration into the EU and NATO, which most Georgians support, but relations with the West have deteriorated as the government has moved closer to Russia and China.

economy.heading: Economic structure
paragraphs: Georgia's economy has grown strongly since the 2000s, driven by reforms that reduced corruption and simplified business rules. Tourism, transport and logistics (as a corridor between Europe and Central Asia), agriculture (wine, hazelnuts and mineral water such as Borjomi), mining and real estate are key sectors.
Remittances are important, and since 2022 an influx of Russians and money flows have boosted growth. The currency is the lari. Unemployment and rural poverty remain challenges.
